items.stem: Solve 3x + 7 = 22.
Explain why you must do the same operation to both sides of an equation.
items.answer: An equation is a balance: both sides are equal, so to keep them equal any change to one side must be made to the other.
items.markingKey: B1 balance/equality; B1 same operation keeps it true [2]

items.stem: Explain how you can check a solution to an equation.
items.answer: Substitute the value back into the original equation and check that both sides give the same number.
items.markingKey: B1 substitute; B1 both sides equal [2]

items.markingKey: Multiply both sides by 4.

items.stem: Explain why multiplying both sides of (x + 2)/3 = (x − 1)/2 by 6 is a useful first step.
items.answer: 6 is the lowest common multiple of the denominators, so it clears both fractions: 2(x + 2) = 3(x − 1).
items.markingKey: B1 LCM of denominators; B1 removes fractions [2]

items.stem: Hana solves 3x + 3 = 9 by dividing both sides by 3 first to get x + 3 = 3, then x = 0. Explain the mistake and solve the equation correctly.
items.answer: Dividing by 3 must divide every term, including 3. Subtract 3 first: 3x = 6, so x = 2.
items.markingKey: B1 must divide all terms (or subtract first); B1 x = 2 [2]

items.stem: Sipho solves (x + 1)/3 = 4 by writing x + 1 = 4 ÷ 3. Explain the mistake and find the correct solution.
items.answer: To remove the division by 3 you multiply both sides by 3: x + 1 = 12, so x = 11.
items.markingKey: B1 multiply (inverse of divide); B1 x = 11 [2]

Chloe has $23 and saves $5 each week. Leila has $71 and saves $2 each week. (a) Write an expression for the amount Chloe has after w weeks. (b) Form and solve an equation to find the number of weeks after which they have the same amount. (c) Find the amount each of them has at that time.
Factorise completely 6x + 15.
items.markingKey: HCF of 6 and 15 is 3.

items.stem: Explain what "factorise completely" means, using 12x + 18 as an example.
items.answer: Take out the highest common factor so the bracket has no further common factor: 12x + 18 = 6(2x + 3), not 2(6x + 9).

items.stem: Explain how to check that a factorisation is correct.
items.answer: Expand the brackets; the result should be the original expression.
items.markingKey: B1 expand; B1 compare with original [2]

Factorise x² − 49.

items.stem: Factorise x² + 7x + 12.
Explain why x² + 9 cannot be factorised as a difference of two squares.
items.answer: It is a sum, not a difference, of two squares; (x + 3)(x − 3) gives x² − 9.
items.markingKey: B1 sum not difference; B1 (x + 3)(x − 3) = x² − 9 [2]

items.stem: Leila factorises x² − 10x + 21 as (x + 7)(x + 3). Explain the error and give the correct factorisation.
items.answer: The middle term is negative, so both numbers must be negative: (x − 7)(x − 3). Expanding (x + 7)(x + 3) gives +10x.
items.markingKey: B1 sign of middle term requires negative numbers; B1 (x − 7)(x − 3) [2]

items.stem: Ethan factorises x² − 11x + 28 as (x + 4)(x + 7). Explain the error and give the correct factorisation.
items.answer: The middle term is negative, so both numbers must be negative: (x − 4)(x − 7). Expanding (x + 4)(x + 7) gives +11x.
items.markingKey: B1 sign of middle term requires negative numbers; B1 (x − 4)(x − 7) [2]

items.stem: Explain why rearranging a formula uses the same steps as solving an equation.
items.answer: In both cases you apply inverse operations to both sides, in reverse order, to isolate the required letter.
items.markingKey: B1 inverse operations; B1 both sides / reverse order [2]

items.stem: Explain why, when making r the subject of A = πr², you take the positive square root only in a context such as area.
items.answer: A radius is a length, so it must be positive; the negative root has no meaning here.
items.markingKey: B1 length positive; B1 discard negative root [2]

items.markingKey: Divide both sides by 2π.

items.stem: Explain what to do when the new subject appears twice in a formula, such as ax = b + cx.
items.answer: Collect the terms containing x on one side, factorise out x, then divide: x(a − c) = b, so x = b/(a − c).
items.markingKey: B1 collect terms; B1 factorise and divide [2]

items.stem: Leila makes t the subject of v = u + at and writes t = v − u − a. Explain the mistake.
items.answer: a multiplies t, so you must divide by a, not subtract it: t = (v − u)/a.
items.markingKey: B1 a is a multiplier, so divide; B1 t = (v − u)/a [2]

items.stem: Lina rearranges A = πr² to get r = √A/π. Explain the mistake and give the correct formula.
items.answer: Divide by π before taking the square root, so π must be inside the root: r = √(A/π).
items.markingKey: B1 π inside root; B1 r = √(A/π) [2]

items.stem: Explain why you should define the letter you use when forming an equation from a problem.
items.answer: It makes clear what the unknown represents (e.g. "let x be the width in cm"), so the solution can be interpreted correctly in context.
items.markingKey: B1 states meaning/units; B1 interpret answer [2]

items.stem: Explain why a solution of x = −4 might be rejected when x is the width of a rectangle.
